Great paper from Google on making ML experiments reproducible for coding agents.

(bookmark it)

If you run agents on research code, this one is worth your time.

They find that refined artifacts raise agent reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% across four models and cut API spending by 19.7%.

ReproBridge turns one successful reproduction into a package the next agent can reuse. The package holds the cleaned code, the environment setup, scripts that launch each experiment, and a written guide.

A new agent reruns the experiment from that package. A separate auditor then checks that the runs actually happened.

The benchmark covers 1,029 tasks from 36 papers, each with five human-verified reference scores. The gap between the best and worst model drops from 21.6 to 3.9 points. Removing the code or the environment setup causes the largest losses.

If your agents keep failing to rerun a repo, save the setup steps from the first successful run before trying a bigger model.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08452

Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/reprobridge-building-reproducibility-into-ml-research-artifacts-2611.08452

"dumb zone" a little more flexible for 1m frontier models. I usually my autocompact to 400k and tend to do a manual compact between 200-400k depending on model/harness. less so clearing now

3-tier subagent architectures make this a little better too. You can have a top level orchestrator that runs the process, and can launch subagents that can themselves launch subagents. So instead of human steering two levels, top level can. 

i don't think there's any good reason to go beyond 3-levels of subagent nesting today for majority of tasks.

YMMV, as always these are guidelines / training wheels. your intuition as to whether model is on track or getting dumb is always the best source!

If you're only working on vulnerability management, then you're only focusing on 1/3 of the problem.

If you prioritize breaking the attack paths around lateral movement and abuse of authorized access, then you're addressing all of the major attack vectors at once (vulnerabilities, phishing, stolen credentials, social engineering, software supply-chain, etc).

People love to focus on finding and fixing vulnerabilities because it feels good in the same way that running laps around a circular track feels good. You're moving fast and having predictable, repeatable tasks, but not actually getting anywhere.

Hey, I work at Anthropic. We understand why this email can be confusing. This is about Cathedral's unauthorized access through third-party software we use, which was reported on Oct 26: https://x.com/logangraham/status/2114849047953670635

Notices like these usually don't name the other party, so ours didn't either. But we can see how that made it harder to tell what it was about.

Cathedral reached business contact info and account details like name, email and plan, but not prompts, outputs or payment details. We contained the affected systems the same day we became aware of it and worked with the vendors to close the vulnerabilities.

We know there's more to do, and we're continuing to improve how we secure and monitor the third-party software we use.

给 Agent 装 MCP 之前，先认清一件事：mcp.json 本质上是可执行配置 🫠

不是「装个插件方便点」，是把「能跑命令、能读文件、能出网」的权限写进仓库。过去公开过相关 CVE：有人用提示词注入写 cursor/mcp.json，有人换掉已批准的命令不再弹窗，还有 PR 自带 mcp.json 在 CI runner 上直接跑。

装之前过一遍这 7 条（可收藏）👇

1️⃣ 先盘点：本机 + 仓库里所有 MCP 配置
Cursor：cursor/mcp.json、~/.cursor/mcp.json
Claude Code：mcp.json、~/.claude.json

2️⃣ 当代码审：给 mcp 配置加 CODEOWNERS，改配置必须过审

3️⃣ 密钥别落盘：用环境变量引用
· Cursor：${env:NAME}
· Claude Code：${VAR}

4️⃣ 钉死版本：禁止裸 npx -y 某包，写清版本号再过审

5️⃣ CI 只信 base 分支：别让 PR 自己决定加载哪些 server
· Claude Code：--strict-mcp-config + 只传白名单
· 流水线：从 base 还原 mcp.json，别 checkout 后直接信 head

6️⃣ 批准绑「整条命令」，不绑「server 名字」
名字可以冒充，command/args 换了必须重新批准

7️⃣ 不信任的本地 stdio：断外网再跑（deny all / 沙箱）
读得到文件 + 出得了网 = 经典外传组合

你现在仓库里有几个 mcp.json？评论区报个数也行 👀

Lydia Hallie's post this week undersells what's actually happening: if you were using Conductor, you can do many of the same things with Claude Code Projects now. That's not a feature comparison. That's a platform absorbing a category that venture money had just finished funding.

Conductor raised a 22 million dollar Series A this year, led by Spark and Matrix, to build exactly this: parallel Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor agents running in isolated git worktrees on your Mac, so none of them step on each other's changes. It's a six person company out of Y Combinator's 2024 batch. Claude Code Projects, which Anthropic relaunched in September, does the same core job inside Anthropic's own cloud: pick up branches, run agents in parallel, review what they did. Early reports note it burns through usage limits noticeably faster than single-session Claude Code, which tells you the compute cost of running several agents at once isn't an implementation detail. It's the actual price of the category.

Conductor isn't alone outside Anthropic's walls. Emdash supports twenty-plus agents with issue tracker integration built in. Tembo targets enterprise teams with signed commits and bring-your-own-key billing. Crystal lets you A/B test the same prompt across agent runs. All of them solve a problem that didn't exist two years ago. Not can an agent write this function, but how do I supervise five of them without losing track of what each one touched.

I've watched this shape before, in cloud infrastructure. The fight stopped being about which VM you rented and became about who owned the orchestration layer on top of it. Docker didn't lose to Kubernetes because containers got worse. It lost the layer that mattered, because Kubernetes owned the dashboard. Claude Code Projects doesn't need to beat Conductor's editor. It just needs to be the default surface people open first, because it's already where the agents live.

The thing nobody's pricing in: if Anthropic absorbs the orchestration layer the way AWS absorbed container orchestration, every startup building a nicer way to run multiple coding agents is building a feature, not a company.

180 Agent Skills for Google Cloud, Apache 2.0, one GitHub command to install. That's google/skills, and it picked up 534 stars in a single day on its way past 22,900.

Run npx skills add google/skills and an agent gets working knowledge of Agent Platform, Gemini API, Genkit, GKE, BigQuery, AlloyDB, Spanner, Cloud SQL, IAM, Security Command Center, Google Ads, and Analytics, about 180 skills in total. Each one is a folder with a SKILL.md file and YAML frontmatter an agent can scan without loading the whole thing into context. There are matching plugin installs for Claude Code, Codex, and Google's own Antigravity CLI.

That frontmatter format isn't Google's. Anthropic published it as an open spec earlier this year, and it already sits inside Microsoft's SharePoint and Teams integrations, Cursor's editor, Atlassian, Figma, and OpenAI's own Codex CLI, which added support for it back in October. Google is simply the biggest name yet to build 180 skills on someone else's packaging format instead of inventing its own.

MCP went the same way first. Anthropic open sourced that too, and it now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation with every major lab plugged in, xAI and Google included despite neither originating it. Skills looks like it's heading down the same road, one dependency at a time, and the lab that writes the format spec is quietly becoming the one every other lab's agents run on top of.

HOW TO LET CLAUDE CODE CODEX OR CURSOR CONTROL YOUR DESKTOP APPS

Vercel just open-sourced agent-desktop. your agent no longer stays inside the terminal. it can click and type in real apps on your machine.

the play: install agent-desktop > connect it via MCP to Claude Code / Codex / Cursor > give it a task that needs the desktop > watch it run in the background

steps:

1. clone the repo  
   https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop

2. run the setup so your agent can see the accessibility tree of open apps (Notes, Reminders, browsers, etc.)

3. start Claude Code, Codex or Cursor and ask it to do something that requires the desktop (update a reminder, fill a form, debug an app)

4. leave it running. it works in the background while you do other things. multiple agents can run at the same time, each with its own cursor.

> the catch  
it needs real desktop permissions. once you give them, the agent can click anything the logged-in user can click.

> what not to do  
do not run it with full permissions on a machine that has production logins or secrets open. start with a test user or a clean session.

you asked it to help with the work. now you are the one watching the screen.  
bookmark this and reply with what desktop task you would hand off first.

Your AI coding agent might be installing dead software, and you’d never know 👻

Security researchers at Glow Labs studied real AI coding sessions and found something worrying.

When you ask an agent like Claude Code, Cursor or Codex CLI to “set up GitHub,” it often installs an old, retired MCP server instead of the official one.

It isn’t your fault, either. 98% of the time, the AI picked the old package from memory. The user never asked for it.

Here’s why it matters:
- Retired MCP packages have been downloaded 17.3 million times since July 2025
- 4 high-severity security flaws, and no fixes are coming
- Your security tools (SCA, EDR) can’t see it

They’re calling it MCPhantom!

Swipe through to see how it happens and the 4 quick fixes your team can make today. 👉
